title: Potty training
intro: Potty training is the process of helping a child learn to use the toilet. Children are ready at different ages, usually between about two and four years. Staying relaxed, watching for signs of readiness and avoiding pressure usually leads to the best results, and accidents are a normal part of learning.

sections.heading: Signs of readiness
paragraphs: Children are usually ready when they stay dry for a couple of hours, show interest in the toilet, can follow simple instructions, can pull clothes up and down, notice when they need to go, and show discomfort in dirty nappies. Bowel and bladder control are tied to the child's nervous system maturing, so starting too early often only prolongs the process.

sections.heading: Getting started
paragraphs: Choose a calm period without major changes such as a new sibling or moving house. Offer a potty or a child-sized toilet seat with a stool for the feet. Let the child get used to it, sit clothed first, and introduce regular sits after meals. Use easy-to-remove clothing and explain simply what to do. Praise efforts and keep a relaxed attitude.

sections.heading: Handling accidents
paragraphs: Accidents are normal, particularly when the child is busy, ill or excited. Stay calm, clean up without blame and encourage trying again. Punishment, shaming and pressure can cause fear and withholding of stools. Night-time dryness comes later, often years after daytime control.

sections.heading: Common difficulties
paragraphs: Some children refuse the potty or hold back stools, which can lead to constipation and pain. Offer fibre, water and relaxed toilet times, and stop training for a while if needed. Constipation or pain with passing stool needs medical advice.

sections.heading: When to seek advice
paragraphs: Speak to your paediatrician if your child is over four and still not daytime dry, has sudden regression after being trained, burning with urination, constant dribbling, very frequent urination or ongoing constipation. Bedwetting after age five or six is common and often runs in families, and help is available if it troubles the child.

examples.title: Setting up a routine
examples.text: Imagine your two-and-a-half-year-old shows interest in the toilet. You could introduce the potty after meals, give praise for sitting even without success and keep spare clothes nearby.

examples.title: Responding to refusal
examples.text: Suppose your child cries each time you mention the potty. You might pause for a few weeks, avoid pressure and try again when they seem ready.
